content: Medical treatment for subfertility primarily involves the use of ovary-stimulating drugs. These include selective estrogen receptor modulators (SERMs) like clomiphene citrate, gonadotropins, gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH) agonists and antagonists, and human chorionic gonadotropin. These drugs may exert their effects directly or indirectly on the endometrium, which is the lining of the uterus. It is well-established that nulliparity (having no children) and certain causes of subfertility are recognized risk factors for endometrial cancer. The objective of this study was to evaluate whether the use of ovary-stimulating drugs for subfertility treatment is associated with an increased risk of endometrial cancer. A comprehensive search of multiple databases, including CENTRAL, MEDLINE, and Embase, was conducted up to July 2016. Additional searches were performed in OpenGrey, ProQuest, ClinicalTrials.gov, ZETOC, and major conference reports. No restrictions were placed on language or publication status. The study included cohort and case-control studies that examined the relationship between endometrial cancer and exposure to ovary-stimulating drugs in adult women with subfertility. Data extraction and analysis were performed independently by pairs of reviewers. Inconsistencies between studies were quantified using the I² statistic, and random-effects models were used to calculate pooled effect estimates. Separate analyses were conducted to compare subfertile women treated with ovary-stimulating drugs to both the general population and untreated subfertile women, in order to account for subfertility as an independent risk factor for endometrial cancer. Nineteen studies, involving a total of 1,937,880 participants, were included in the analysis. The overall quality of evidence was rated as very low due to significant risks of bias and indirectness, as most studies were non-randomized. Six studies that included only subfertile women, without a general population control group, found no significant association between exposure to any ovary-stimulating drug and the risk of endometrial cancer (relative risk [RR] 0.96, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.67 to 1.37; 156,774 participants; very low-quality evidence). However, fifteen studies that used the general population as a control group reported an increased risk of endometrial cancer following exposure to ovary-stimulating drugs (RR 1.75, 95% CI 1.18 to 2.61; 1,762,829 participants; very low-quality evidence). Five studies specifically examined the use of clomiphene citrate in subfertile women (92,849 participants). The pooled analysis suggested a positive association between clomiphene citrate exposure and endometrial cancer risk (RR 1.32, 95% CI 1.01 to 1.71; 88,618 participants; very low-quality evidence). This association was particularly evident at high doses of clomiphene citrate (greater than 2000 mg) (RR 1.69, 95% CI 1.07 to 2.68; two studies; 12,073 participants) and with a high number of treatment cycles (more than seven cycles) (RR 1.69, 95% CI 1.16 to 2.47; three studies; 13,757 participants). Four studies compared subfertile women treated with clomiphene citrate to the general population and found an increased risk of endometrial cancer (RR 1.87, 95% CI 1.00 to 3.48; four studies; 19,614 participants; very low-quality evidence). However, it remains unclear whether this increased risk is due to the underlying conditions requiring clomiphene citrate treatment, such as polycystic ovary syndrome, or the drug itself. When using untreated subfertile women as controls, exposure to gonadotropins was associated with an increased risk of endometrial cancer (RR 1.55, 95% CI 1.03 to 2.34; four studies; 17,769 participants; very low-quality evidence). However, a separate analysis of two studies (1,595 participants) comparing gonadotropin exposure to the general population found no significant difference in risk (RR 2.12, 95% CI 0.79 to 5.64; very low-quality evidence). Exposure to a combination of clomiphene citrate and gonadotropins, when compared to untreated subfertile women, did not show a significant difference in endometrial cancer risk (RR 1.18, 95% CI 0.57 to 2.44; two studies; 6,345 participants; very low-quality evidence). However, when compared to the general population, an increased risk was observed (RR 2.99, 95% CI 1.53 to 5.86; three studies; 7,789 participants; very low-quality evidence). This suggests that subfertility itself, rather than the treatment, may be the primary factor contributing to the increased risk. In conclusion, the current evidence is of very low quality and does not allow for definitive conclusions. However, there appears to be an association between clomiphene citrate use and an increased risk of endometrial cancer, particularly at high doses and with prolonged use. This increased risk may be largely attributable to underlying conditions, such as polycystic ovary syndrome, rather than the drug itself. The evidence regarding gonadotropin exposure remains inconclusive.
